messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Ali, a 27-year-old Middle Eastern man and physical therapist, was assaulted one night while walking home from work. The event was sudden and unexpected: he heard footsteps behind him and turned to see a figure wearing cologne that overwhelmed his senses, followed by a violent attack. Since then, Ali has been struggling with the haunting memories of that night, particularly when exposed to similar triggers. The assault had left physical scars as well; the pain in his body serves as another potent reminder of what happened. Whenever he experiences physical discomfort or is near someone wearing cologne, Ali’s mind immediately flashes back to the traumatic event. The olfactory and somatic cues trigger a cascade of negative emotions, reinforcing his belief that he will never be able to feel normal again. This belief has left him feeling isolated from his wife and cautious in his interactions with patients. Ali had come to believe that he can't rely on himself anymore—a notion that is exacerbated each time he encounters a familiar scent or feels pain. These triggers not only remind him of the event but also reinforce his negative appraisals, making it increasingly difficult for him to trust his own judgment and reactions. What frightens Ali most is the constant fear that any reminder could bring back those feelings of helplessness. The sense of vulnerability has left him hyper-vigilant. He starts at unexpected movements or touch from others, reacting with alarm even in situations where there is no real threat. This startle response is a direct result of his negative appraisals and the constant fear that another attack could happen again. The more he feels threatened, the more he relies on maladaptive strategies like dissociation to cope. He often finds himself pretending that the event happened to someone else, which allows him to momentarily escape from the overwhelming emotions tied to the trauma. This dissociative behavior becomes a cycle; whenever Ali experiences a trigger, his mind immediately shifts away from reality, reinforcing the notion that he can't trust himself and amplifying his sense of threat. The maladaptive strategies also contribute to maintaining his triggers. By constantly checking his body for signs of danger or injury, Ali inadvertently keeps the memory of the assault alive. This hyper-focus on physical sensations only intensifies his startle response and heightens his overall state of alertness, making it increasingly difficult for him to relax. Ali’s work as a physical therapist has been affected by these symptoms. He avoids patients who wear cologne or have body positions that remind him of the attack. His avoidance behavior has strained his relationships with colleagues and patients alike, leading to a sense of isolation at work. The combination of negative appraisals, triggers, and maladaptive strategies has created a self-reinforcing cycle that feels almost inescapable. What finally brought Ali to seek help was an incident where he had a severe startle response during a therapy session with a patient wearing cologne, which led him to abruptly leave the room. He realized that his symptoms were interfering with his ability to function professionally and personally. Despite feeling ashamed of what happened to his body and fearing further attacks, Ali is most hopeful for finding ways to regain control over his life and rebuild trust in himself. Ali’s journey through trauma has left him grappling with a complex web of emotions and behaviors, but he remains determined to seek support and break the cycle that continues to torment him.
